_comment: The grading vocabulary: the single source of truth for both scales.
Everything that names a grade is generated from this file - app.js's label tables,
build-site.py's, the methodology page, llms.txt, and the ClaimReview ratings.
Edit a label or definition here and run scripts/build.py; nothing else needs touching.
Adding or removing a grade is a code change, not an entry change: it also needs a
v-<slug> pill colour in styles.css, which the build will tell you about.
Array order is display order (strongest to weakest / most to least AI-driven).
source_kinds is not a third grade. It classifies a *link*, not a result: nothing
scores or ranks an entry by it. The categories describe the role a link plays and
never who published it - a lone researcher announcing their own result on X is an
announcement exactly as a corporate press release is. Medium is irrelevant; who is
speaking, and what they are doing, is the whole question.

verification.label: Formally verified
verification.definition: A machine-checked proof (Lean, Coq, Isabelle) or an exact symbolic or computational verification that anyone can rerun. The gold standard.

verification.label: Independently checked
verification.short: checked by third parties who were not the authors
verification.definition: Multiple qualified people unaffiliated with the announcing lab have checked the result and confirmed it.

verification.label: Peer reviewed
verification.definition: Published in a venue with real review. Weaker than a formal proof for mathematics, but stronger for empirical claims.

verification.label: Author verified
verification.short: verified only by the people who produced it
verification.definition: The human collaborator checked it, but no independent party has confirmed it yet.

verification.label: Claimed
verification.definition: Announced but not yet checked by anyone outside the lab. The default for a press release.

verification.label: Disputed
verification.short: substantive public challenge to the result
verification.definition: Substantive technical objections have been raised and remain unresolved.

verification.label: Already known
verification.rating_label: Already known: correct but not novel
verification.short: correct, but the result already existed in the literature
verification.definition: The result turned out to already exist in the literature. These entries stay on the record; showing the failure mode is what makes the rest trustworthy.

autonomy.label: Autonomous
autonomy.short: the AI did it without human problem-setting or steering
autonomy.definition: The AI produced the core idea and the result with no human mathematical input beyond posing the problem.

autonomy.label: AI-led
autonomy.short: the AI produced the core idea; humans framed or checked it
autonomy.definition: The AI produced the key insight; humans formalised, checked, or cleaned it up.

autonomy.label: Collaborative
autonomy.short: genuine back-and-forth between AI and human
autonomy.definition: Genuine back-and-forth. Neither party would have gotten there alone.

autonomy.label: AI-assisted
autonomy.short: humans led; the AI helped with parts
autonomy.definition: A human drove the research; the AI accelerated search, algebra, or literature review.

autonomy.label: Search scaffold
autonomy.short: a human-built search harness (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) with an LLM inside
autonomy.definition: The AI is a component inside a human-designed search loop (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve). The system found it, but the framing was human.

autonomy.label: Retrieval
autonomy.short: the AI located an existing result rather than producing a new one
autonomy.definition: The AI surfaced an existing result humans had overlooked. Valuable, but not new mathematics.

source_kinds.label: Original work
source_kinds.short: the paper, proof, code or data itself
source_kinds.definition: The work itself: a paper, preprint, formal proof, dataset or code repository - something a reader can open and check. Not what was said about the work, but the work. Any grade stronger than Claimed has to rest on one of these.

source_kinds.label: Announcement
source_kinds.short: the claim as first made public, by whoever made it
source_kinds.definition: The claim as first made public by the people behind it - a company press release, a research blog post, or an individual's own post on a personal site or social media. What matters is that it is first-party, not that an organisation published it: a single researcher announcing their own result belongs here. This is the claim framed by the people with the most at stake in it.

source_kinds.label: Media coverage
source_kinds.short: news and press reporting on the claim
source_kinds.definition: News and press reporting written by journalists rather than by the people who did the work. Coverage restates a result for a general audience, and the restatement is often where it acquires a stronger meaning than its authors gave it.

source_kinds.label: Independent commentary
source_kinds.definition: An independent write-up by someone who neither produced the result nor is reporting it as news - a researcher's blog post, an expert explainer, a detailed thread. Often the most informative link on an entry. It may support the claim, complicate it, or both; commentary arguing the result is wrong is a challenge instead.

source_kinds.label: Challenge
source_kinds.definition: The case against: a critical review, a rebuttal, a failed replication, or a citation of prior work showing the result was already known. The strongest challenge is listed first. A challenge disputes the claim, not the people who made it.
